title: Enums, const enums, and union alternatives
hook: TypeScript enums look familiar to C# developers, but they generate run-time JavaScript objects with surprising behavior. Many teams now prefer literal unions and `as const` objects instead.

blocks.text: An **enum** declares a set of named constants. **Numeric enums** auto-increment from 0 (or a start value) and support **reverse mapping** (number → name). **String enums** have no reverse mapping. **`const enum`** is erased at compile time — members are inlined as literals (no run-time object). Modern TypeScript style often replaces enums with **literal unions** (`"pending" | "done"`) or **`as const` objects** for zero run-time overhead and better tree-shaking.

entries.plainDefinition: Enum with number values. Auto-increments unless explicitly set. Supports reverse mapping.
Enum where each member has an explicit string value. No reverse mapping.
Compile-time only enum. Values are inlined; no run-time object is emitted.
A type alias of string or number literals replacing an enum with no run-time code.

blocks.text: Enums are one of the most debated features in TypeScript. They generate an Immediately Invoked Function Expression (IIFE) at run time for numeric enums — unexpected bundle size. Reverse mapping lets you look up enum names from numbers, which is rarely needed and confuses deserialization. C# enums are lightweight value types with clear semantics; TypeScript enums are a code-generation feature with quirks. The TypeScript team itself recommends avoiding enums in new code when literal unions suffice.

blocks.title: Modern alternative
blocks.body: Prefer `const STATUS = { Pending: "pending", Done: "done" } as const; type Status = typeof STATUS[keyof typeof STATUS];` — single source of truth, no run-time enum object, full tree-shaking.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Numeric enum
items.body: Members get auto-incremented numbers. `Status.Pending` is 0. `Status[0]` reverse-maps to "Pending".

items.title: String enum
items.body: Each member needs an explicit string initializer. No auto-increment, no reverse mapping.

items.title: const enum
items.body: Inlined at compile time. Cannot be used with `isolatedModules` + transpile without `preserveConstEnums`.

items.title: Literal union replacement
items.body: Define allowed values as a type. Use `as const` object when you need both values and types.

diagram.title: Enum vs union alternative
diagram.source:
flowchart LR
  subgraph runtime ["Run-time cost"]
    NE["numeric enum"] -->|"generates IIFE object"| JSOBJ[JS object]
    SE["string enum"] -->|"generates object"| JSOBJ
    CE["const enum"] -->|"inlined literals"| NONE[No object]
    UNION["literal union + as const"] -->|"zero overhead"| NONE
  end

snippet.label: Numeric enum with reverse mapping
snippet.code:
enum Priority {
  Low,       // 0
  Medium,    // 1
  High,      // 2
}

const p: Priority = Priority.High;  // 2
const name = Priority[2];            // "High" — reverse mapping
snippet.explanation: Lines 1–5: numeric enum auto-increments from 0. Line 7: member access gives the number. Line 8: reverse mapping looks up the name from the number — unique to numeric enums, often surprising.

snippet.label: String enum and const enum
snippet.explanation: Lines 1–4: string enum — explicit values, no reverse mapping. Lines 6–9: const enum — values inlined at compile time. Line 11: no run-time CacheTTL object exists in the output JavaScript.

snippet.label: Union alternative — recommended pattern
snippet.explanation: Lines 1–5: `as const` object is the single source of truth for values. Line 7: derive the union type from the object. Lines 10–12: use STATUS.Done for autocomplete without a run-time enum object. Tree-shakeable and JSON-friendly.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Using numeric enums for API status codes — JSON can deliver invalid numbers that pass the type check. Relying on reverse mapping in production code. Using const enum with `isolatedModules` without `preserveConstEnums`. Mixing enum and union styles in the same codebase.

blocks.text: The TypeScript compiler emits an IIFE for numeric enums that creates a bidirectional object — this is why bundlers cannot tree-shake unused members. `erasableSyntaxOnly` (TS 5.8+) flags enums as non-erasable syntax, pushing teams toward unions. For flags/bitfields, C# `[Flags]` enums map poorly to TypeScript — use numeric literals with bitwise ops or a dedicated library. When interviewing, state your preference (union + as const) and acknowledge enums are valid when interoping with C# backends that serialize numeric enums.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying enums are identical to C# enums. Not knowing numeric enums generate run-time code. Unable to articulate the union alternative. Ignoring JSON deserialization risks with numeric enums.

interviewTakeaways: Numeric enums auto-increment and support reverse mapping — generate run-time IIFE.
const enums are inlined; literal unions have zero run-time cost.
Prefer as const objects + derived union types in modern code.
60s: Enums generate JS objects unlike C#. Use literal unions for new code. String enums for string values. Validate JSON at boundaries.
Follow-up: what is erasableSyntaxOnly and how does it affect enums?
commonPitfalls: Defaulting to numeric enums without mentioning run-time cost.
Not knowing reverse mapping exists on numeric enums.
Strong answer: 'Unions + as const for new code. Enums when interoping with numeric APIs. Always validate deserialized values.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript has no enum keyword. TypeScript enums compile to JavaScript objects (except const enum). Plain objects or string constants are the JS equivalent.
C# enums are value types with clear integer backing. TypeScript numeric enums add reverse mapping and generate objects — behavior differs significantly.
